title: US Retail Sales Rebound 1.2% in August as Consumers Keep Spending
excerpt: Shoppers stepped up purchases of cars and back-to-school goods in August, Commerce Department data showed Wednesday, underscoring a resilient economy just as the Federal Reserve moved to raise interest rates.
body:
• Retail sales jumped 1.2% in August to $773.9 billion after a revised 0.5% July decline, the Commerce Department said Wednesday — beating economists' forecast of 0.8%.
  • Core retail sales, which feed into GDP estimates, surged 1.4% against expectations of 0.4%, lifting third-quarter growth estimates above a 2.0% annualized rate.
  • The data landed hours before the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate for the first time in three years, to roughly 3.9%, in a fight against stubborn inflation.
  • Gasoline at $4.37 a gallon and consumer prices up 3.4% year over year show households spending through real pressure — though economists warn fuel costs could crimp future spending.

American shoppers came back in force in August. Retail sales rose 1.2% last month, the Commerce Department said Wednesday, powered by motor vehicle purchases and back-to-school stocking that more than reversed July's first spending decline in nine months.

The rebound beat the 0.8% gain economists polled by Reuters had forecast; estimates ranged from 0.2% to 1.1%. July's figure was revised to a 0.5% drop from a previously reported 0.6% decline.

Context & Background

July's pullback had raised questions about whether consumers were finally tiring after a summer of heavy spending around the World Cup and Amazon Prime Day. Economists largely wrote it off as a blip: Prime Day and related promotions shifted from July to June this year, draining July's figures, according to Reuters and Dow Jones Newswires.

The August data supports that reading. Nonstore retailers — including online sellers — saw sales rise 2.6% after a sharp July decline, and spending at electronics and appliance stores climbed 1.6%. Bank of America data showed credit and debit card spending per household rose 0.9% month over month in August after a 0.2% July decline. Higher gasoline prices flattered the headline by lifting station receipts, but even excluding gas stations, sales rose 1.1%, the Associated Press reported.

Impact & Analysis

The so-called control group — which strips out autos, gasoline, building materials and food services and maps most closely to consumer spending in GDP — surged 1.4% after a 0.4% July decline, against expectations of 0.4%. Steady wage growth and recent stock market gains are supporting spending, Reuters reported, with households also saving less. The August jobs report added to the picture: employers added 162,000 jobs, well above forecasts, after a labor market that had wobbled through much of the summer.

"This reaffirms that the economy is more than capable of handling higher interest rates, providing the Fed plenty of scope to hike to get inflation under control."

— Bradley Saunders, North America economist, Capital Economics

Consumers are not spending blindly. Retailers reporting quarterly results in recent weeks said shoppers have grown more selective and are seeking lower-priced goods, while consumer sentiment deteriorated this month. Mark Mathews, chief economist at the National Retail Federation, said he is seeing the economy's K-shaped spending trends soften — higher-income households' wealth gains no longer diverging as sharply from lower-income households' struggles.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-American households and investors, the read-through is mainly financial. A Fed that hikes means higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards over time, while savers may see better deposit yields. Strong US consumer demand also underpins corporate earnings broadly — relevant for retirement portfolios tilted toward American equities.

What's Next

The Fed's quarter-point increase, the first in three years, came the same day as the retail report, with policymakers eyeing one more increase by year's end. Consumer prices rose 0.4% from July to August — quadrupling the previous month's 0.1% — and were up 3.4% from a year earlier.

"The economy is healthy enough to withstand a few rate hikes, keeping the Federal Reserve's attention firmly on the upside risks to inflation."

— Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist, Oxford Economics

The risk ahead is gasoline. The average price of regular rose to $4.37 a gallon Wednesday, according to AAA — about 47% more than the less than $3 it cost before the US-led war with Iran. Diesel is up 68%. "If gas prices remain high, then you know you have to start questioning where the consumer is going to fund that spending growth from," Mathews said. Pearce warned of "a renewed squeeze on real incomes" and a deeper bifurcation of the consumer in coming months.
